title: Composition, the urn, and printing
short: Written in May 1819; the urn is imaginary, a composite of Greek art Keats knew from the British Museum and engravings.
body: Like the other spring odes, this was written in May 1819. No single vase matches Keats's description; editors point to the Townley Vase and the Elgin Marbles (which Keats saw with Haydon and celebrated in a sonnet of 1817) in the British Museum, the Borghese Vase and the Sosibios Vase, of which Keats traced an engraving from Henry Moses's collection of antique vases (the tracing is at Keats House). Ian Jack also proposes paintings by Claude for the sacrificial procession. It was first printed anonymously in the Annals of the Fine Arts for 1819 (the issue is dated variously to late 1819 or January 1820), then in the 1820 volume.

title: still unravish'd bride
short: 'Still' means both 'yet' and 'motionless, silent': the urn is a bride whose marriage is never consummated.
body: The pun on 'still' governs the poem. The urn has not yet been violated (by time, breakage or interpretation) and it is also quiet and unmoving. A bride 'unravish'd' is perpetually on the threshold of consummation, like the lovers on its side. Cleanth Brooks made the double meaning central to his New Critical reading: the urn is both a figure of arrested life and of enduring permanence. 'Ravish' can also mean to enrapture, so the urn is also not yet carried away.

anchor: foster-child of silence and slow time
title: foster-child of silence and slow time
short: The urn's real parents (its makers) are gone; silence and time have reared it since.
body: The urn's original potter and painter are long dead; it has been adopted and brought up by silence and the slow passing of centuries. The genealogical metaphors (bride, foster-child, then historian) give the object three successive identities in the first three lines. 'Slow time' suggests both duration and the way time seems to move slowly or not at all for the figures on the urn.

title: Sylvan historian
short: The urn tells a story of woodland scenes, but a history without names or dates.
body: 'Sylvan' means of the woods; the urn is a historian because it records a 'flowery tale', but its history is rustic and pictorial. Cleanth Brooks took the phrase for the title of his essay 'Keats's Sylvan Historian: History Without Footnotes' (1947), arguing that the urn's kind of truth is that of an imaginative, not factual, record. The claim that it tells its tale 'more sweetly than our rhyme' sets up the competition between visual art and poetry that the poem stages.

title: leaf-fring'd legend
short: The story on the urn, framed by a border of painted leaves.
body: Greek vases often bear bands of foliage ornament around their scenes. 'Legend' carries both its senses: a story (often of saints or heroes), and, from its Latin root, an inscription or caption to be read. The legend 'haunts about' the shape, as if the story were a ghost lingering round the vessel; the urn is figured as something both present and spectral.

anchor: Tempe or the dales of Arcady
title: Tempe; Arcady
short: Two ideal Greek landscapes: the vale of Tempe in Thessaly and pastoral Arcadia in the Peloponnese.
body: Tempe is a gorge in Thessaly between Mounts Olympus and Ossa, through which the river Peneus runs; it was famous in classical poetry for its beauty and associated with Apollo. Arcady (Arcadia), a mountainous region of the central Peloponnese, became through Virgil's Eclogues and Renaissance pastoral the ideal country of shepherds and love. Keats's question cannot be answered: the urn's place is the idealised Greece of literary tradition rather than a real location.

title: the questions
short: A rush of unanswered questions animates the frozen scene and introduces its erotic violence.
body: Stanza 1 ends in seven questions, which the urn, being silent, cannot answer. They describe a Bacchic or Dionysiac scene: pursuit, 'maidens loth' (unwilling), struggle, music and 'wild ecstasy'. The frenzy contrasts with the 'quietness' of the first line. Vendler reads the stanza as the first of the speaker's several attempts to interpret the urn, each partial; the questions return in stanza 4 about the sacrifice.

title: timbrels
greek: Old French timbre, Latin tympanum, Greek tympanon, 'drum'
short: Tambourines or hand-drums, instruments of ecstatic dance.
body: A timbrel is a small hand-drum or tambourine. The word is strongly biblical: Miriam takes 'a timbrel in her hand' and the women follow her 'with timbrels and with dances' (Exodus 15:20). On Greek vases the tympanon and the double pipe (aulos) accompany Dionysian revels. The pipes reappear as 'soft pipes' in stanza 2, now silenced by art. The list of pipes and timbrels prepares the paradox of silent music that opens stanza 2.

title: Heard melodies ... those unheard
short: Imagined music is sweeter than actual music, because it plays 'to the spirit' rather than the 'sensual ear'.
body: The paradox has a Platonic flavour: the ideal is superior to its sensory embodiment. 'Ditties of no tone' are songs without sound. The idea also recalls Keats's letter to Bailey (22 November 1817) on the imagination's power to anticipate a greater happiness, 'repeated in a finer tone' hereafter. Critics debate how far the poem endorses this claim; by stanza 3 the advantage of the unheard and unchanging is shadowed by its coldness.

title: Bold Lover
short: The lover will never reach the kiss, but neither will his love fade nor his beloved age.
body: The consolation is double-edged: arrested at the moment of desire, he will 'for ever' love and she 'be fair', but he will never have his 'bliss'. The repeated 'never, never' and 'for ever' set up the tension between frustration and permanence that the poem never fully resolves. Brooks saw here the urn's paradoxical truth; others, such as Earl Wasserman, read the poem as a dramatized movement towards and away from an ideal 'region' of permanence.

title: happy, happy
short: The insistent repetitions of stanza 3 have been read as a failure of tact or as a deliberate sign of strain.
body: 'Happy' occurs six times in the stanza and 'for ever' four times. Many critics (beginning with the earlier twentieth-century commentators surveyed by Bate) have thought the stanza the weakest in the ode; others argue that the overinsistence is dramatic, showing the speaker trying too hard to believe in the urn's happiness until the last three lines collapse into human 'breathing passion' and its aftermath. 'Still to be enjoy'd' again puns on 'still': yet to be, and for ever.

title: high-sorrowful and cloy'd
short: Human passion ends in satiety and fever, with a burning forehead and parched tongue.
body: 'Cloy'd' means surfeited, sickened by excess of sweetness. Real love, unlike the urn's, is consummated and so passes into satiety and sorrow; its physical symptoms ('burning forehead', 'parching tongue') resemble those of fever, perhaps of consumption, which Keats had watched in Tom. The stanza thus turns the urn's advantage into a criticism of human life, but it also reminds us that the urn's figures cannot breathe.

title: the sacrifice
short: A religious procession leading a garlanded heifer to a 'green altar', recalling the Parthenon frieze.
body: The scene of a heifer led to sacrifice is very close to the south frieze of the Parthenon among the Elgin Marbles, where a heifer raises its head as it is led; Keats had seen the marbles repeatedly. Ian Jack also points to Claude's painting of the sacrifice to Apollo. The heifer 'lowing at the skies' is the one sound-image of the stanza; the 'silken flanks' with garlands evoke the sacrificial ritual. The 'mysterious priest' and 'green altar' are left unexplained, as befits the urn's silence.

title: little town
short: The town not shown on the urn is imagined emptied for ever, its people frozen in procession elsewhere.
body: The town is the speaker's invention: it is not depicted on the urn but inferred from the procession. Because the figures can never return, the town must remain 'desolate' for ever, with 'not a soul to tell' why. Many readers find this the poem's most haunting moment, where the logic of artistic permanence produces a permanent absence. Vendler sees in it the speaker's growing awareness of the cost of the urn's eternity.

title: Attic shape! Fair attitude!
short: The urn as an Athenian form and as a pose; the near-pun on 'Attic' and 'attitude' has divided critics.
body: 'Attic' means Athenian, hence classically pure and restrained. 'Attitude' meant the posture of a figure in art (OED), a term of painting and sculpture. The jingle between the two words has been judged a lapse by some readers and a deliberate sound-play by others. The stanza turns from inside the urn's scenes back to the object as a whole. The exclamations mark the speaker's withdrawal from involvement with the figures to contemplation of the whole object.

title: brede; overwrought
short: 'Brede' is an old form of 'braid', an interwoven pattern; 'overwrought' means decorated over, and over-excited.
body: Keats's 'brede' is a variant spelling of 'braid', used of embroidery or interlacing; it describes the frieze of figures running round the vase. 'Overwrought' means 'worked over' (the surface is wrought with marble men and maidens), but its other sense, 'excessively agitated', recalls the 'mad pursuit' and 'wild ecstasy' of stanza 1. Note too 'marble': the urn of the poem seems to be carved rather than painted, like the Townley or Borghese vases.

anchor: dost tease us out of thought
title: tease us out of thought
short: The urn draws us beyond the bounds of thought, as eternity does.
body: Keats had used the phrase in his verse Epistle to J. H. Reynolds (March 1818): 'Things cannot to the will / Be settled, but they tease us out of thought'. 'Tease' combines teasing out (as with wool) and provoking. The urn, like eternity, frustrates reasoning: it cannot be grasped by discursive thought. RPO glosses it as drawing us beyond the limits of thought.

sources.cite: Representative Poetry Online (Univ. of Toronto), 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', ed. J. R. MacGillivray, line notes

title: Cold Pastoral!
short: The urn is a pastoral scene that is permanent but lifeless; the epithet qualifies the poem's praise.
body: A pastoral is a representation of idealised rural life; 'cold' is both the literal coldness of marble and the absence of human warmth. The phrase gathers the poem's ambivalence: the urn is a 'friend to man' but cannot share 'breathing human passion'. Critics who read the ode as finally sceptical about art (e.g. those who stress the 'desolate' town) put weight on this epithet; others see it as part of a balanced, both/and attitude.

title: Beauty is truth, truth beauty
short: The most debated lines in Keats: who speaks them, to whom, and whether they mean anything, are all disputed.
body: In the Annals of the Fine Arts the last two lines had no quotation marks; in the 1820 volume the five words are quoted, so the urn speaks them and the rest is ambiguous (urn or poet; addressed to readers or to the urn's figures). The transcripts by Keats's friends differ again. Keats had written to Bailey (22 November 1817) that 'What the imagination seizes as Beauty must be truth'. Bridges admired the lines; Quiller-Couch thought them vague; I. A. Richards treated them as a 'pseudo-statement'; T. S. Eliot called them 'a serious blemish on a beautiful poem' (1929); Cleanth Brooks defended them as a speech 'in character' for the urn. Some later critics read the final clause as the poet's qualification.
